notes.meaning: Paul asks whether Christians should keep on living in sin so that God's grace—his free favor to the undeserving—can increase even more. Since God forgives sin so generously, some people wrongly claimed that more sin gives God more opportunities to show his mercy. Paul raises this bad idea so that he can tear it down right from the start.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern hyper-grace teachers argue that because grace always covers sin, believers do not need to be concerned about continuing in sin or striving to obey God.

notes.meaning: Paul answers the question with a shocked refusal, saying this must never be. A true believer has died to sin, meaning its guilt and ruling power over the heart have been broken. A person cannot be dead to a sinful way of life and still make a regular home in it.

Baptism pictures a believer being joined with Jesus Christ in his death and burial. Just as the Father's glorious power raised Christ from the grave, believers are brought out of death to walk in a brand-new way of life. The water shows that our old life of sin is buried for good so that we can follow God.

differ.view: Baptism is an outward symbol of a spiritual union that already took place through faith, and it is properly shown by dipping under water to portray burial and resurrection.
Baptism is a covenant sign and seal that truly conveys grace to God's chosen people, though the physical rite itself does not save.
Baptism is a means of grace through which God works the forgiveness of sins and new spiritual life, including for infants.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Baptism is a sacrament that actually washes away original sin, joining the soul to Christ and infusing the new life of grace.

notes.meaning: Believers are joined tightly to Jesus, like a branch grafted into a tree. Because they share in a death like his, they are certain to share in the power of his resurrection. This bond guarantees that they receive spiritual life right now and will be raised to glory later.

Our old sinful self was nailed to the cross with Christ so that the ruling power of sin would be destroyed. Because that corrupt nature was dealt a death blow, Christians are no longer trapped as helpless slaves to sin. God breaks the grip of the cruel master that once directed our choices.

differ.view: The crucifixion of the old self is a gradual dying process in which the believer's corrupt nature is weakened and put to death over time.
The death of the old self is a completed, once-for-all historical fact achieved by Christ, distinct from the daily struggle against remaining fleshly desires.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Baptism cancels the guilt of original sin, but an inner inclination toward evil remains to be fought against with God's help.

notes.meaning: When a slave dies, his earthly master loses all claim and control over him. In the same way, the Christian who has died with Christ is declared free from the rule and guilt of sin. Death cancels the old master's right to issue commands.

Since Christians have died with Christ by turning away from sin, they believe they will also share in his life. This shared life begins here as a holy walk with God and reaches perfection in heaven. Trusting Christ connects a person to his never-ending life.

Jesus rose from the dead and will never face death a second time. When he gave himself up on the cross, death had temporary power over him, but his resurrection broke that power forever. Because death no longer has any claim over Jesus, his victory stands firm for all time.

Jesus died to sin once and for all as an atonement—a sacrifice to pay the penalty for sin. His single death achieved everything needed to break sin's power. Now that he is risen, he lives an unending life dedicated fully to the glory of God.

Believers must view themselves in the very same light. They should count themselves as truly dead to the rule of sin, but alive to God through Christ Jesus. True faith accepts what God has done and begins living solely to please him.

Believers are commanded not to let sin sit on the throne of their frail human bodies. The physical body will one day die, but it does not have to obey sinful desires right now. Christians are urged to stand against evil cravings instead of letting them run their daily lives.

Christians must not hand over their hands, feet, or tongues as weapons for doing wrong. Instead, they should offer their whole being to God like people who have been brought from death to life. Every part of the body should be dedicated as a tool for doing what is right and honoring to God.

Sin will not be the ruler over Christians because they are not under law, but under grace. The law demanded complete obedience without giving inner strength to keep it, which left people helpless under its curse. Grace gives free forgiveness and the Holy Spirit's power, guaranteeing that sin cannot keep its hold.

Paul asks if being free from the law and under God's grace gives people permission to commit sins here and there. He rejects that idea completely. Finding mercy and love from God is the strongest possible reason never to treat sin lightly.

When a person willingly chooses to obey someone, they become that person's actual slave. Obeying sinful desires makes someone a slave to sin, which ends in eternal death. On the other hand, obeying God makes someone a servant of righteousness, which leads to life and holiness.

Paul thanks God because the believers have left their old slavery to sin behind. They have wholeheartedly obeyed the true pattern of Christian teaching given to them. That message acted like a mould, shaping their thoughts and desires into the likeness of Christ.

Christ has set believers free from the cruel grip of sin. Yet being released does not mean people can just do whatever they feel like. Instead, they have been gladly transferred into the service of righteousness, living to do what is good.

Paul uses the picture of masters and slaves to help readers understand because human thinking can be slow to grasp spiritual truth. Just as they once used their bodies to chase dirty and unlawful desires, they must now offer themselves to righteousness. This wholehearted service leads to practical holiness in everyday life.

Back when they were slaves to sin, believers felt free from any obligation to do what is right. They did not let God's commands guide them, and they had no interest in pleasing him. That so-called freedom was actually total spiritual bondage to evil.

Paul challenges them to look back and ask what good fruit they ever harvested from their sinful past. Those deeds produced nothing worthwhile and only bring feelings of deep shame today. Worse still, the final destination of that way of living is eternal death.

Now that believers have been set free from sin and have become servants belonging to God, they harvest real fruit. That fruit is sanctification, which means being made clean and holy in everyday life. The final outcome of this journey is everlasting life in the presence of God.

Death is the earned wage that sin pays out, meaning eternal punishment is what evil actions truly deserve. In sharp contrast, eternal life cannot be earned or deserved; it is the completely free gift of God. This wondrous gift comes only through union with Jesus Christ our Lord.
